newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian analysts dismiss 1997/98 cocoa pessimism.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian analysts dismiss 1997/98 cocoa pessimism.

text.p: Crop analysts say concerns over scant cocoa tree flowering for the 1997/98 Ivorian main crop (Oct-April) and talk of a blitz on harvests from the dry El Nino weather forecast for late 1997 are exaggerated.
One analyst told Reuters on Monday after trekking around cocoa plantations there was no cause for pessimism.
"There are more fruits and flowers than at this time last year. I have seen excellent setting," he added, putting April flowering at record levels based on his own annual tree sampling data.
London-based trader E D and F Man in a May report said "due to unfavourable weather, early setting for the new crops in West Africa has been the lowest since 1983".
Other local analysts also dismiss pessimistic reports and say updated crop forecast figures will soon land on traders' desks.
"We are now in the silly season," said one, referring to an annual occurrence of widely divergent crop estimates, which are usually given more colour in July before a clear picture emerges in August.
Comparisons between data from different years and from different sources can be misleading at this time of year, they said.

"The main crop set late last year. Are we ahead or just on time this year? I am not yet sure but there are more fruits on the trees," one told Reuters. "Everyone's sample is different so it's best to wait a little longer."

Swiss chocolate giant Callebaut Barry, which owns two cocoa processing factories in Ivory Coast, in early June put the 1997/98 Ivorian crop at 1.1 million tonnes, not far below the 1995/96 record of 1.2 million tonnes.
But weather fears look set to continue amid speculation over the potential effects of dry El Nino weather recently forecast by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
Local analysts say the effect, presuming the weather pattern even materialises in West Africa, could be negligible.

"If the El Nino develops and hits in late 1997 there will be no effect on the cocoa. The main crop (Oct-April) will already be on the trees," one said recently. "If there is a drought late in the year it will not matter too much.
Cocoa pods for main harvests develop from flowers over the preceding May-to-August period.

"In April we had the flowers (for October)," one crop analyst said on Monday, adding that his set of data showed record levels. "In May cherelles appeared and now in June we have plenty of (pod) fruits."

A particularly harsh July and August dry season could cut down potential harvest volumes, said one analyst, adding that July 1996 rains had been twice as heavy as the long term average and that 1997 had (so far) been satisfactory.
"You only have to look out of your window to see there is no El Nino yet," he said.

"Rains for the first 15 days of June (1997) have already matched the long-term average for the whole month although early May was a bit drier than usual." said another. "We must now wait and see how the small dry season turns out in July and August."
Analysts foresee no effects on an expected July peak to the 1996/97 mid-crop, which has been put at anything between 100,000 tonnes and close to last year's 200,000.
Exporters put carryover of stocks from the 1995/96 mid-crop season into the 1996/97 main crop at between 40-60,000 tonnes.
-- Abidjan newsroom, + 225 21 90 90
